title: the DSG improving-play opener

banner.title: The DSG IMPROVING PLAY OPENER: EXPEDITION PLANNING, BEASTS OF BURDEN, WATERCRAFT, R528: printed pp. 59-60 (pdf 60-61) - the frame (game habits causing problems, the recommendations grouped into expedition planning, speeding play, and effective fighting) and the expedition planning: the success or failure often determined before leaving base - more often the failure - so learn everything possible first (NPC interviews, the approaches and periphery, magic for insight, even rumors having a basis in fact, the basilisk slithering meaning mirrors); scout with light avoid-combat parties (one or two thieves, invisibility spells, gaseous-form potions) and keep scouting during the adventure (the listening-at-doors function, one character looking before the group enters, cutting ambush risk and raising tactical options); and the type-of-expedition preparation - objectives, duration and areas considered, ready to climb or descend cliffs, cross water, provide light, feed for an extended period and still return, extra food for opportunity, foot travel on the rough going, waterways the easy fast access for boaters but notoriously dangerous and unpredictable (the placid stream turning cascade or vanishing crack), beasts of burden where smooth; the mules: 2,000 gp of evenly distributed saddlebag weight no encumbrance, 6,000 gp maximum at 1/2 speed refusing over eight hours a day, the 50% persuadable six-foot-or-less chasm (never wider, never loaded over 2,000, no mind-changing on failure), average-steepness stairs and human footing with hands-required slopes too steep, the 50% very-steep slope, the 90% willing swim and six-foot jump into water (refusing over 2,000 gp), the 3-inch-per-round swim, the string following its leader (a refused leader unhitched, never changing its mind), the strange-odor jitters at 25% bolt/bray/freeze/normal (one check for the group), and the 360-ft stone noise muffled to 90 ft with leather or cloth boots replaced daily; the dogs: the 100-lb war-dog varieties (shepherds, malamutes, wolfhounds), trained per the animal-trainer proficiency, 200 gp without penalty, 500 gp maximum at half speed and -4 to all attacks, no swimming or steep climbing over 200 gp, the 50% attack-strangers tendency (restrained dogs barking instead), the advanced-training discipline (no attack or bark unless directed, hand signals needing sight), and the keen-smell-and-hearing darkness penalties of -2 instead of -4; and the watercraft: the kayak nimblest and roughest-capable but requiring small-boat proficiency from all characters, larger craft carrying more together but limited in rough or narrow waters, the collapsible boat flexible but bulky and less sturdy, waterborne scouting the more vital (the waterway ascertained ahead, the one-way current needing a return plan)
banner.provenance: the DSG scan (archive.org item advanced-dungeons-dragons-1st-edition), pdf = printed + 1; the text read from the IA djvu OCR (djvu.txt lines ~7564-7848) with the pdf Acrobat-Capture layer as the second read (idx 137 = the printed p. 59 window, idx 139 = the printed p. 60 window); the compiled-tables appendix has no reprint of this prose. A CLEAN-READ ROUND: both machine reads agree on every load-bearing number - the mule 2,000/6,000 gp with the half-speed and 8-hour rules, the 50% chasm at six feet, the 50% very-steep slope, the 90% swim, the 3-inch swim rate, the 25% odor quartet, the 360/90-ft noise, the dog 200/500 gp with the -4, the 100-pound weight, the 50% stranger attack, and the -2-not--4 darkness. The only garbles are the standing glyph classes (djvu "5096" reading as 50%, the "üsing" lead). SEAMS: the Monster Manual mule and war dog definitions (cross-book), the animal-trainer proficiency (R506/R527), the small-boat proficiency (R518 water travel), and the R526 collapsible boat. The improving-play chapter split per the content-density rule: this round covers children 142-144 (the planning opener), and R529 takes fighting effectively, diversions, speeding play, creative spell use, languages and mapping (children 145-150). Nothing auto-credits.
banner.sentinel: A prose round: no tables pin. The numbers pin as consts per the R508 convention: the mule weights (2,000 free, 6,000 max), the half-speed divisor and 8-hour cap, the 50% chasm at 6 ft and the 50% steep slope, the 90% water willingness with the 6-ft jump, the 3-inch swim, the 25% odor quartet, the 360/90-ft noise, the dog weights (200/500 gp, 100 lbs), the -4 overload penalty, the 50% stranger attack, and the -2 darkness penalty. The rest pins as prose bools: the three-category frame, the early-determined success, the scouting and rumor rules, the expedition preparation, the transport tradeoffs, the mule string/footing/stairs rules, the dog training and discipline, and the watercraft comparisons. The Monster Manual, R506/R527, and R518/R526 seams are noted; nothing auto-credits.

DESCRIPTIONS, printed p. 58 (pdf 59) - the fourteen brief
introductions: the animal trainer (little beyond
harnesses and leashes, but a great deal of outdoor room,
with shelter and food if boarding), the armorer (a small
forge, several hammers, at least one small anvil and
metal files, with good ventilation and exhaust for the
especially hot fire the armor irons demand), the
blacksmith (the armorer's equipment in greater
assortment and size, but cruder iron needing
lower-quality tools), the boatwright (a major investment
at a carefully chosen launchable location - excepting
kayaks, canoes and small rowboats - with the space the
boat size plus 10 feet in all directions, the tools all
carpentry plus pitch or tar), the bowyer/fletcher
(little beyond knives and vises), the carpenter
(hammers, spikes, axes, and chisels), the gem cutter
(finely tooled chisels, hammers and vises, good light,
sturdy safes or strongboxes), the leatherworker
(punches, needles, knives, scissors, and treating oils),
the miner (a shallow pan and container for stream
panning, but picks, shovels, shoring timbers, hammers,
spikes and mining carts for a tunnel, the need growing
with the tunnel), the potter (the kiln limiting the wares),
the smelter (the efficient high-temperature furnace, the
individually operated bellows, and the iron-buckets-on-
rails or cauldron/stone-trough feeding system), the
stonemason (going where the work is, with a sturdy wagon
and oxen), the weaponsmith (a small blacksmith's shop
plus the fine finishing tools for edges and
ornamentation), and the weaver (a very small area, the
spinning wheel and loom). A CLEAN-READ ROUND. A LOSSLESS

consts.name: dnipMuleFreeWtGp
consts.comment: up to 2,000 gp of weight, evenly distributed in saddlebags, does not encumber a mule.

consts.name: dnipMuleMaxWtGp
consts.comment: a mule carries up to a maximum of 6,000 gp at half speed.

consts.name: dnipMuleOverHalfSpeedDiv
consts.comment: a mule loaded over 2,000 gp travels at 1/2 speed.

consts.name: dnipMuleMaxWalkHours
consts.comment: an overloaded mule refuses to walk for more than eight hours a day.

consts.name: dnipMuleChasmPct
consts.comment: there is a 50% chance that a mule can be persuaded to jump a chasm six feet wide or less - and it never jumps a wider gap, and never while carrying more than 2,000 gp.

consts.name: dnipMuleChasmMaxFt
consts.comment: the persuadable chasm is six feet wide or less.

consts.name: dnipMuleSteepPct
consts.comment: there is a 50% chance that a mule can be persuaded to climb or descend a very steep slope.

consts.name: dnipMuleWaterPct
consts.comment: there is a 90% probability that a mule is willing to swim or jump into water - though it refuses to enter water carrying more than 2,000 gp.

consts.name: dnipMuleJumpHeightFt
consts.comment: a mule jumps from a height of up to six feet to enter water.

consts.name: dnipMuleSwimInches
consts.comment: a swimming mule travels at a rate of 3 inches (30 feet) per round.

consts.name: dnipMuleOdorPct
consts.comment: an odor-alarmed mule bolts (25%), brays in panic (25%), freezes in place (25%), or functions normally (25%) - a single check for a whole group of mules.

consts.name: dnipMuleNoiseFt
consts.comment: mules walking on stone make noise audible to a distance of 360 feet.

consts.name: dnipMuleMuffledNoiseFt
consts.comment: leather or cloth boots wrapped around the hooves reduce the audible distance to 90 feet - the muffles must be replaced daily.

consts.name: dnipDogFreeWtGp
consts.comment: a trained dog fitted with small saddlebags carries up to 200 gp without penalties to movement or combat.

consts.name: dnipDogMaxWtGp
consts.comment: a dog can be loaded with up to 500 gp of weight.

consts.name: dnipDogOverloadAtkPenalty
consts.comment: an overloaded dog moves at half speed and suffers a -4 modifier to all attacks - and cannot swim or climb steep slopes over 200 gp.

consts.name: dnipDogWeightLbs
consts.comment: the war-dog varieties described generally weigh about 100 pounds.

consts.name: dnipDogStrangerPct
consts.comment: dogs have a 50% chance to attack anything that does not belong to their party unless physically restrained - restrained dogs that would attack instead bark loudly and savagely.

consts.name: dnipDogDarkPenalty
consts.comment: a dog's penalties for attacking, damage, and AC in complete darkness are all -2 instead of the normal -4.

bools.name: dnipThreeCategories
bools.comment: the improving-play tactics are grouped into three categories: expedition planning, speeding play of the game, and effective fighting.

bools.name: dnipSuccessDeterminedEarly
bools.comment: the success or failure of an expedition is often determined before the party leaves base - more often the failure, from a neglected vital feature, an essential piece of equipment, or missing information.

bools.name: dnipLearnEverythingFirst
bools.comment: before leaving, characters should make strong efforts to learn everything possible about the setting: NPC interviews, exploring the approaches and periphery, and using magic for insight.

bools.name: dnipRumorsHaveBasis
bools.comment: even rumors should not be disregarded, for such talk often has a basis in fact - basilisk rumors mean wise characters bring mirrors.

bools.name: dnipScoutLightAvoidCombat
bools.comment: a scouting mission comprises characters traveling much more lightly than normal, avoiding combat at all costs - one or two thieves, possibly aided by invisibility spells, potions of gaseous form, or other magical protection.

bools.name: dnipScoutDuringAdventure
bools.comment: scouting continues during the adventure: listening at a door before smashing it is a scouting function, and at least one character should look at an area before the whole group enters - reducing ambush risk and increasing tactical options.

bools.name: dnipExpeditionPlanningNeeds
bools.comment: an underground expedition of any length needs considerable planning: the objectives, the length of time, and the areas to explore all considered, with the objective ideally a task motivating the PCs.

bools.name: dnipPrepareForTerrain
bools.comment: the PCs must be prepared to climb or descend cliffs, cross water by swimming or boat, provide light sources, feed themselves for an extended period, and still return to the surface.

bools.name: dnipExtraFoodCarried
bools.comment: smart adventurers carry more food than needed, so opportunities for further adventuring are not restricted by supply considerations.

bools.name: dnipRoughGoingOnFoot
bools.comment: if the going is extremely rough - steep descents and narrow passages - the characters must travel on foot, carrying everything in backpacks.

bools.name: dnipWaterwaysEasyAccess
bools.comment: waterways often provide easy access to underground regions: boating characters carry more equipment and travel faster than walkers.

bools.name: dnipWaterwaysDangerous
bools.comment: underground waterways are notoriously dangerous and unpredictable - a placid stream can become a churning cascade or disappear through a crack, blocking exploration.

bools.name: dnipMuleMostCommon
bools.comment: mules are the most commonly employed beasts of burden - somewhat reliable supply mounts that walk as far as any character.

bools.name: dnipMuleStairsAndFooting
bools.comment: a mule walks and climbs stairways of average steepness or a little steeper, keeping its footing as well as a human - but a slope requiring hands is too steep.

bools.name: dnipMuleStringLeader
bools.comment: mules in a string all follow the leader: if the leader performs a task the others automatically follow, and a refusing leader can be unhitched for the next mule to be checked - the old leader never changes its mind.

bools.name: dnipMuleOdorJittery
bools.comment: mules tend to be very jittery at strange smells, and a party employing mules can always be followed.

bools.name: dnipDogWarDogVarieties
bools.comment: the dogs described are all varieties of the war dog (per the Monster Manual), resembling large German shepherds (Alsatians), malamutes, or wolfhounds.

bools.name: dnipDogTrainingRequired
bools.comment: a dog must have animal-trainer proficiency training before serving as a pack animal, and can negotiate slopes of the same steepness as a mule.

bools.name: dnipDogAdvancedDiscipline
bools.comment: a dog with successfully completed advanced training is much more disciplined - not attacking or barking unless directed by its master, and trainable to hand signals it must see to obey.

bools.name: dnipDogKeenSenses
bools.comment: dogs have no infravision, but their keen senses of smell and hearing aid them in darkness.

bools.name: dnipKayakMostNimble
bools.comment: the kayak is certainly the most nimble craft, capable of handling the roughest water - but all characters must have small-boat proficiency for a kayak expedition to succeed.

bools.name: dnipLargerCraftTradeoff
bools.comment: larger craft have greater cargo capacity and keep the PCs together in one boat, but much more limited utility in rough or narrow waters.

bools.name: dnipCollapsibleTradeoff
bools.comment: collapsible boats allow flexible planning, carried overland for stretches, but are bulky and difficult to carry for long distances and not as sturdy as other vessels.

bools.name: dnipWaterScoutVital
bools.comment: if a waterborne expedition is planned, scouting becomes even more important: the nature of the waterway must be ascertained as far ahead as possible, and if a current is relied upon one way, some other means of return must be arranged.
